title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache (Mariner Payments)
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Mariner Payments through Optimize recommendations focusing on batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce token cost while meeting sub-200ms p95 latency goals. Discussion covered cache hit rates, warmup strategies, batching window tradeoffs, and a modeled cost comparison for hosted vs dedicated with quantized model variants. Action items include benchmark run, share pricing + security docs, and follow-up pilot proposal.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-02 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~44m
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Kapoor, Elena Voss / Alex Rivera, Maya Chen, Samir Patel, Renee Gomez

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick intros - I'm Jordan on the account team at Redwood, with Priya and Elena on the Optimize/SE side.
[00:14] Alex: hi all, alex here, head of platform at Mariner - thanks for doing this, excited to see caching and batching stuff.
[00:21] Priya: great, quick agenda, we'll run through batching basics, prefix vs KV cache, show a cost model, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:30] Maya: sounds good. we care about p95 < 200ms and reducing token spend - we've seen costs spike with chat history.
[00:42] Jordan: perfect, that's exactly what Optimize helps with - we'll focus on where to trade latency for cost safely.
[01:12] Priya: so first, batching - two levers, batch size and batching window. bigger batches = better GPU utilization but added queuing latency. for Mariner's traffic pattern (bursty morning, steady evenings) we usually recommend adaptive windowing.
[01:40] Alex: what's adaptive windowing mean in practice? do we add queuing or do dynamic thresholds?
[01:52] Priya: both; Redwood's runtime can look at concurrency and dynamically extend window by up to 30-80ms to pull in more requests when QPS is high, otherwise it falls back to immediate dispatch. so tail latencies remain controlled.
[02:10] Samir: is that per-route? we have some routes that are high-value small-turns.
[02:18] Elena: yes per-route configs - you can set SLOs per route and a routing policy, e.g., high-priority checkout route gets minimal batching, analytics route uses aggressive batching.
[02:40] [transcription glitch: "per route gets minimal batching" -> "per rut...minim batching"]
[03:05] Priya: next, prefix caching vs KV cache. prefix cache is automatic for repeating prefixes - it's great if your app repeats the same prompt starts. KV cache is more explicit: store and reuse key-value KV state for long-running conversations to avoid recomputing attention keys.
[03:30] Maya: we've attempted local caching but it's been messy - our sessions vary a lot, many prefixes differ by small tokens like user ids.
[03:45] Priya: canonicalization helps - strip variable tokens (user ids), normalize timestamps, then you get much higher hit rates. often 2-3x hit rate improvement after simple canonicalization.
[04:05] Alex: any risks for correctness when canonicalizing?
[04:12] Priya: yes, if the variable token affects semantics you can accidentally change outputs. we recommend a whitelist of fields safe to canonicalize and run evals. Redwood Optimize has a small evaluation harness to test canonicalization impact on quality.
[04:40] [00:04:50-ish: background noise, Renee typing]
[05:05] Elena: a typical cost model slide - we model token cost per request = generation tokens * model cost + overhead. then we layer in cache hit rate and batching uplift. here's an example: with a 40% cache hit rate and 1.8x batching throughput uplift, unit cost drops ~45%.
[05:28] Samir: what's your baseline model? are you assuming an 8-bit quantized Mistral variant?
[05:35] Priya: in customer examples we show both FP16 and quantized int8 variants. for the demo we used a quantized 7B variant to show conservative numbers. quantization affects latency lightly but can cut GPU costs a lot.
[05:50] Maya: do you support multiple model variants in a fallback chain? e.g., if dedicated capacity is full degrade to hosted cheaper model?
[05:58] Jordan: yep, smart routing - you can set policy to route to cheaper variant or different region when capacity constrained. automatic fallback preserves availability.
[06:20] [06:20] Alex: let's talk concrete numbers - our current average request is 90 tokens input + 60 tokens output. we're at roughly 120k requests/day.
[06:35] Priya: ok with 120k/day and that token size, we can run a quick back-of-envelope: assuming $0.03 per 1k tokens baseline, and 40% cache hit, plus batching 1.8x you could see cost per request drop from ~0.005 to ~0.0028. that's 40-50% reduction. (numbers simplified)
[07:05] Samir: can you share the model spreadsheet? we'd like to plug our exact token distribution.
[07:12] Jordan: yes we'll share the workbook; Priya will send a template.
[07:20] Priya: now, KV cache specifics - KV cache stores the attention keys/values client-side or in a managed cache layer? Redwood manages it in the serving layer and can optionally expose a TTL-configured cache you can persist for sessions.
[07:40] Maya: curious about memory footprint - if we store KV for many sessions what's the RAM impact?
[07:48] Elena: kv entries scale with sequence length and layers, so we recommend TTLs or LRU eviction. in our benchmarks for 8k context models, a warm session took ~30-40MB of KV, but hit rates yielded huge savings for multi-turn chat.
[08:15] [08:15] Renee: security question - where is KV stored and is it encrypted at rest?
[08:22] Jordan: by default Redwood-managed KV is encrypted at rest and in transit; for Private/Dedicated customers we offer VPC placement and KMS integrations so keys never leave customer control.
[08:40] Renee: do you have SOC2 docs?
[08:44] Jordan: yes, we'll send SOC2 + ISO attestation as part of the security pack.
[09:05] Priya: back to eviction strategy - shorter TTLs for low-value sessions, longer for engaged users. you can tier KV cache: hot in-memory for active users, warm disk-backed for returning sessions, and cold recompute fallback.
[09:30] Alex: can Redwood's caching touch PII? we need controls for not caching sensitive fields.
[09:38] Priya: you can configure mask/skip rules so fields flagged as sensitive are excluded from cache keys; we also support customer-side token scrubbing before sending.
[09:58] Samir: about the benchmark you mentioned - what's involved?
[10:04] Jordan: typically we run a 2-4 hour benchmark on a representative subset; we do two passes: baseline with your current calls, and then with caching + batching config. we measure p50/p95, throughput, GPU utilization, and cost model delta.
[10:26] Maya: we have rate limits and an API gateway in front, any extra considerations?
[10:31] Elena: we recommend either bypassing gateway for benchmark or increasing rate limits for the test window, plus we instrument request headers so Redwood can map to per-route SLOs.
[10:50] [transcription note: "bypass" -> "by pass" occasionally]
[11:05] Priya: now a quick demo - (screen share) here's the Optimize console: per-route latency heatmap, cache hit analytics, suggested configs. you can see suggested batching window changes and expected cost delta.
[11:30] Alex: can you show the suggestion for our sample dataset?
[11:36] Priya: for the sample trace you provided (thanks!) the console suggested canonicalization + 250ms window on low-priority routes and near-zero window on checkout. expected hit rate 38% and cost down ~42%.
[12:00] Maya: the canonicalization rules - are they editable?
[12:05] Priya: yes a rules editor, you can preview changed prompts and run a small eval set to measure semantic drift.
[12:22] Samir: about consistency - if we canonicalize, do we need to regenerate certain outputs to keep state? what about embeddings?
[12:30] Elena: embeddings are separate; you can cache embeddings at the application layer. canonicalization mainly helps with generation paths. regenerate is only needed when canonicalization removes semantic tokens.
[13:00] [13:00] Alex: what about onboarding timeline - we have compliance windows next quarter.
[13:06] Jordan: typical pilot is 4-6 weeks: onboarding and security review (1-2 weeks), benchmark (1 week), pilot rollouts and monitoring (2-3 weeks). for Private/Dedicated adds extra provisioning lead time.
[13:28] Maya: provisioning time for Dedicated?
[13:31] Priya: depends on capacity; typical lead 4-6 weeks if bespoke hardware, but we can do Hosted pilot in days.
[13:40] Samir: cost comparison hosted vs dedicated for us?
[13:44] Priya: we provided a model in the sheet: for sustained workloads (>= 3m RPS sustained) dedicated often wins; for variable traffic hosted + reserved bursts is better. we'll tailor numbers after you share traces.
[14:10] [14:10] Renee: small security follow-up - we need retention policies and audit logs exposure.
[14:16] Jordan: Redwood stores audit logs by default and can increase retention for enterprise add-on; we'll include audit log retention options in the pack.
[14:40] Priya: demo cont - here's cache analytics: per-route hit rate, average reuse length, and top prefixes. you can export the top-100 prefixes to help canonicalization.
[15:02] Alex: seeing top prefixes helps us prioritize work. nice.
[15:10] Priya: also note cold-start behavior - for KV cache warmup we recommend provisioning for the first 48-72 hours of pilot to build a meaningful cache and avoid skewed metrics.
[15:33] Maya: how do you measure cache effectiveness? do you simulate session returns?
[15:38] Elena: we compute hit rate, reuse factor, and average saved tokens per hit. we also run A/B on quality to ensure canonicalization doesn't regress.
[16:00] [16:00] Samir: micro question - do you support model quantization automatically or is that a manual onboarding step?
[16:08] Priya: we have curated quantization profiles; we recommend a small validation set to choose profiles. Redwood can handle compilation and kernel selection as part of onboarding.
[16:25] Alex: are there any cases where caching hurts quality?
[16:31] Priya: yes, when prompts include dynamic context that changes answer intent. that's why we have TTLs and policy-based eviction and the eval harness to catch regressions.
[16:50] Jordan: quick real-customer story - one payments customer saw 55% cost reduction after canonicalizing the payment confirmation prompts and 1.6x batching uplift.
[17:05] [17:05] Maya: that aligns with what we hope.
[17:15] Priya: ok, now the cost model specifics - we took your sample traces and ran scenario A (hosted + default batching) vs scenario B (hosted + canonicalization + KV + 1.8x batching) vs scenario C (dedicated quantized). scenario B reduced unit cost ~48%, scenario C reduced ~62% but required commit.
[17:45] Samir: curious about SLA differences for dedicated.
[17:50] Jordan: dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and capacity commitments and isolation; Hosted has good SLOs but less isolation. we'll attach SLA wording in the docs.
[18:12] [18:12] Renee: any compliance gap if we go hosted? data residency concerns.
[18:18] Jordan: Hosted can be region-restricted; for strict residency we recommend Private. we'll include residencies supported.
[18:35] Alex: what's the typical cache eviction TTL you recommend for payments flows?
[18:40] Priya: for highly-sensitive flows maybe short TTLs (5-15 minutes) and for engaged support chats 24-48h. it depends on reuse patterns.
[19:00] Maya: are there examples of canonicalization regexes? can you paste a few?
[19:06] Priya: yes - strip account ids like /acct_[0-9]{6}/ replace with <ACCOUNT_ID>, mask timestamps to iso-date-only, etc. we'll send examples.
[19:30] [19:30] Alex: walk me through the proposed pilot scope.
[19:34] Jordan: Pilot scope: 1) instrument 7 days of traffic, 2) run 48h baseline benchmark, 3) apply canonicalization + caching and run benchmark, 4) evaluate quality, 5) roll to 10% traffic for 2 weeks.
[19:55] Samir: fine - cost of pilot?
[20:00] Jordan: Pilot pricing is usually credits + small professional services fee; we'll include line items in the SOW.
[20:20] Priya: technical note - when we do KV cache the runtime stores per-session KV; to avoid memory blowup we can configure per-session max-KV-size, and an LRU across sessions.
[20:40] Maya: any recommended metrics to expose in our dashboards?
[20:45] Elena: expose cache_hit_rate, average_reuse_length, batch_size_mean, latency_p95, and gpu_util. we can push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint.
[21:10] Alex: about function/tool calling - we currently use tool calls often, does cache impact that?
[21:17] Priya: tool calls usually happen after model output; caching helps by saving tokens prior to calls, but if tool output is included in subsequent prompts you'll want to decide whether to include tool responses in cached prefixes.
[21:40] Samir: ok makes sense.
[22:05] Jordan: any blockers for running the pilot?
[22:09] Maya: main blockers: legal needs to see DPA and SOC2, infra needs to confirm VPC access for benchmark.
[22:18] Renee: legal will need encryption details and retention language.
[22:22] Jordan: we'll send the security pack and DPA.
[22:35] Priya: quick note: cache warmup can be accelerated by seeding KV with a subset of your most common prefixes - we can provide a seed tool.
[22:56] Alex: cool.
[23:05] Priya: demo wrap-up - config examples: route A: batching window 250ms, no canonicalization; route B: canonicalization rule set v1 + window 350ms; adjust per SLO.
[23:26] Maya: can we get recommended default rules for our checkout + support flows?
[23:30] Priya: yes, we'll tailor after we see traces.
[23:48] Samir: slight tangent - does Redwood expose token-level cost by user?
[23:54] Jordan: yes, Console exposes token-level cost per-api-key/route and can export granular usage.
[24:20] Elena: also you'll see trace-level analytics for cache hits so you can validate behavior.
[24:40] Alex: very helpful.
[24:55] Priya: any more deep technical questions?
[25:02] Maya: one: how do you handle KV across model upgrades? when we move from model v1 to v2 does KV reuse work?
[25:12] Elena: it's model-dependent - KV formats can change between architectures. Redwood supports KV migration helpers and automatic fallbacks. we recommend a rollout strategy testing KV reuse with small percentage.
[25:40] Samir: great.
[25:55] Jordan: recap and next steps - we'll send pricing/SOW, security pack, Optimize playbook, and the template to upload traces. Priya will propose benchmark dates.
[26:12] Alex: timeline looks good.
[26:20] Renee: we'll review security docs and get back on restrictions.
[26:28] Jordan: thanks - action items noted.
[26:40] Priya: one last tip - often a small canon rule and short TTL yields 30% improvements with near-zero regressions. start small, measure, then widen.
[27:05] Maya: good rule of thumb.
[27:20] Samir: ok let's wrap.
[27:25] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the documents and proposed pilot SOW.
[27:32] Alex: thanks all.
[27:35] Meeting ends (recording stopped).

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-words (K-V cash -> KV cache), some speaker label slips. Full recording available on request.
notes: AE + SE demo focusing on Optimize recommendations for Mariner Payments; multiple security and pilot follow-ups agreed.
